newsitem.title: USA: U.S. senator offers bill pushing renewable energy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senator offers bill pushing renewable energy.

text.p: Electric utilities would have to use more renewable energy and older coal generation plants would have to meet emission caps under a Senate bill introduced Thursday.

The bill offered by Vermont Republican Sen. Jim Jeffords would require that all generation facilities that sell electricity in 2000 start demonstrating that at least 2.5 percent of their annual sales were from renewable energy sources, or buy credits from generators that use renewables.
The minimum requirement would rise gradually to 20 percent by 2020.

The bill also would put all combustion generation facilities with at least a 15 megawatt capacity under a single national standard for emissions of pollutants including nitrogen oxide, sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide.
It provides an emissions credits trading program to help facilities meet the caps.

The bill would establish a National Electric System Benefits Fund from revenue collected from a universal wire charge, limited to 0.2-cent per kilowatt hour of electricity, which it said could raise about $6 billion. The fund would provide matching money for states, utilities and consumers to develop renewable energy sources and promote efficiency.
The bill also would require disclosure provisions on electricity bills with information on generators' energy sources.

"Electric utility deregulation has the potential to save consumers millions of dollars in energy costs. At that same time, deregulation can move us away from reliance on dirty fossil fuels," Jeffords said at a news conference.

"My proposal will cap emissions from generation facilities, forcing old coal plants to meet tighter air quality standards or shut down. We attack pollutants that lead to smog, acid rain, mercury contamination and ground-level ozone," Jeffords said.

Environmental groups, which praised Jeffords' bill, fear that in the increasingly competitive electricity market, utilities will increase use of dirty coal power plants that do not have to comply with emissions limits under current rules.

"Sen. Jeffords' legislation lays the foundation for clean competition in an industry that for too long has imposed excess costs on the country, both economically and environmentally," Daniel Lashof, a senior scientist with the Natural Resources Defense Council, said in a statement.
